title: Some Neural Networks Inherently Preserve Subspace Clustering Structure
claim: Cluster structure survives each transformation step when weights are learned, but random weights destroy it.
layout: 5 heatmap panels in one row, left-to-right, last panel contrasting color
description: A single row of five square heatmaps, each titled with a projection matrix: P(X*), P(X), P(WX), P(Y) with learned W, and P(Y) with random W. The first four panels look nearly identical. Each has a teal background with four bright, speckled blocks along the diagonal, which shows four clusters. The blocks step down from top-left to bottom-right. This shows the clustering structure carries through each stage of the transformation. The fifth panel, with random W, is uniformly dark purple with only faint noise. The block-diagonal structure is gone. The eye goes first to the last panel because its color differs, then compares it with the repeated diagonal pattern in the others. There are no arrows, axes, or legends.
caption: Projection matrices revealing the clustering structure of the data, which is preserved through every step of a ReLU transformation. Lemma 4.1 shows that the projections of X⋆and X are close. Lemma 4.2 shows that the projections of X and WX are close. Lemma 4.3 shows that the projections of WX and Y are close when W satisfies certain conditions that the network encourages through the learning process. In contrast, random W’s destroy the clustering structure.
abstract: It has long been conjectured and empirically observed that neural networks tend to preserve clustering structure. This paper formalizes this conjecture. Specifically, we establish precise conditions for cluster structure preservation and derive bounds to quantify its extent. Through this analysis we are able to show that certain neural networks are learning parameters that preserve the clustering structure of the original data in their embeddings, without the need to impose mechanisms to promote this behavior. Extensive numerical analysis and experiments validate our results. Our findings offer deeper insight into neural network behavior, explaining why certain data types (such as images, audio, and text) benefit more from deep learning. Beyond theory, our findings guide better initialization, feature encoding, and regularization strategies.
